language-model.name: language model
language-model.definition: A model that assigns probabilities to token sequences by predicting each next token from earlier tokens.
language-model.explanation: A language model turns sequence modeling into repeated conditional prediction. For tokens x₁…xₜ, it estimates each probability p(xᵢ | x₁…xᵢ₋₁). Multiplying these conditional probabilities assigns a probability to the sequence; training usually minimizes their summed or averaged negative logarithms. The chapter's bigram embedding model uses only one earlier byte, while later decoder blocks use a longer causal context. Low loss on a tiny training fixture demonstrates fitting, not broad linguistic ability.

n-gram.name: n-gram
n-gram.definition: A contiguous sequence of n specified units, such as bytes, scalar values, or tokens.
n-gram.explanation: The unit must be named because byte, Unicode scalar, grapheme, and tokenizer-token n-grams differ. Counts of adjacent units form a simple conditional language model: a bigram table predicts the second unit from the first. Increasing n adds context but makes the number of possible histories grow rapidly, leaving many unseen. N-grams are useful baselines and diagnostics even when a neural model is used, because their counts expose tokenization, boundary, and data-leakage mistakes.
